It would honestly be a relief to me if the Moon can't be seen right now. I really hope it isn't visible!

I'm in Reykjavik, Iceland at 2026-04-14 12:21 GMT (UTC+0000) (2026-04-14T12:21:00Z in UTC), at latitude 64.1466 degrees and longitude -21.9426 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 34.122 degrees and its azimuth is 159.921 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 18.176 degrees and its azimuth is 200.971 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 11.39 percent illuminated, 39.356 degrees from the Sun, and 375827.9 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Based on the data you provided, the short answer is: **It is highly unlikely that you would be able to see the Moon with the naked eye right now.**

Here is the breakdown of why you can probably breathe a sigh of relief:

### 1. The "Daylight Washout" Effect
Even though the Moon is technically above the horizon (at an altitude of about 18 degrees), it is currently very close to the Sun in the sky (only 39 degrees apart). Because the Sun is at a high altitude (34 degrees) and the sky is "bright daylight," the atmosphere is saturated with scattered sunlight. This creates a high level of "sky brightness" that overwhelms the relatively dim light reflecting off a thin crescent Moon.

### 2. The Phase of the Moon
You mentioned the Moon is only **11.39% illuminated**. This is a very thin waxing crescent. Unlike a Full Moon, which is bright enough to punch through the daylight, a thin crescent lacks the surface area to reflect enough light to compete with the glare of the Sun.

### 3. The Geometry
The Moon is currently at an azimuth of ~201°, while the Sun is at ~160°. This means the Moon is positioned in the sky in a direction that is still heavily influenced by the Sun's position. In many parts of the world, a crescent this thin would be "lost" in the glare of the daytime sky, appearing only as a faint smudge or not at all without binoculars or a telescope.

### 4. Your Location (Reykjavik)
While Iceland has very clear air, which helps with visibility, the sheer intensity of the Sun at 34 degrees altitude during the day is the deciding factor. Unless you have a very specific, clear line of sight and are squinting intensely toward the southwest, the Moon will likely be invisible to the naked eye.

**Verdict:** You can rest easy. While the Moon is technically "up," the combination of its thin crescent phase and the bright daylight makes it extremely difficult, if not impossible, to spot without optical aid.
